doc.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Family, identity and the Two Flowers metaphor
title: Two Flowers on a Stem: the metaphor, the sextet and the Soul Note album
summary: Jang explains the metaphor of Chinese-American identity and the sextet recording with Murray, Newton, Chen, Debriano and Hart, then begins tying it to his father's death.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren

blocks.x: All right. I like the way you describe your own music as two flowers and a stem. Can you elaborate on that for me?

Well yeah. Two flowers on a stem is a metaphor expressing the symbiotic relationship of my cultural identity as a Chinese-American and a way of honoring tradition and encouraging new ideas, new innovation. “Two Flowers on a Stem” is also the name of a work that I composed I think in the early nineties and it’s the title track of the Jon Jang sextet on Soul Note Records, which is a company that’s based in Milano, Italy and a recording company incidentally that promoted a lot of David Murray’s work. And my sextet included David Murray on tenor saxophone and bass clarinet, James Newton on flute, who is my close friend and artist partner that I’ve collaborated with for twenty years now, Jiebing Chen on erhu, whose — the erhu is a Chinese two stringed instrument and she literally reinvented the erhu. Let’s see who else. Santi Debriano, bassist from New Jersey and New York, and of course the great Billy Hart on multiple percussion. So it was an incredible experience. And “Two Flowers on a Stem” features the melody that I wrote for the erhu, and — let’s see how can I express it — it expresses the feeling of conflict becoming tenderness as a desire for beauty and strength. And that resulted out of a tragedy that occurred in my family when my father died in the worst plane disaster over the Grand Canyon in 1956. It made the front page of the New York Times.
